newsitem.title: USA: Federal law opens door to more tax-free farm loans.
newsitem.headline: Federal law opens door to more tax-free farm loans.

text.p: A provision contained in the mininum wage bill signed into law last month by President Bill Clinton is causing a mini land rush by first-time farmers wanting lower-cost, federally tax-exempt loans to purchase farmland.

The federal tax law change allowed for the first time the use of tax-free loans to finance farmland purchases between family members. It also doubled the amount a farmland an individual can own and still be eligible for the loans.

Wayne Nelson, president of Communicating for Agriculture, a rural advocacy group that lobbied for the changes, said applications for the loans have increased in some of the 14 states that operate beginning farmer loan programs. Meanwhile, other states that don't have the programs, such as Ohio and Michigan, have expressed interest in starting one, he added.

David Wirth, executive director of the Illinois Farm Development Authority, which runs one of the most active tax-exempt bond loan programs in the nation, said that prior to the new law, first-time farmers could not use the loans to finance land purchases from relatives.

"We're getting calls every week from grandparents wanting to sell to grandchildren and couldn't use the bond program because of the related party issue," Wirth said. "Now we have another resource to help those farmers."

The new law also expanded the amount of land a beginning farmer can own and still obtain a loan to 30 percent of the median farm size in the county where the land is located. Previously, the limit was 15 percent.
However, the value of the land already owned by the farmer cannot exceed $125,000, according to Wirth.

Under Illinois' program, the authority issues a tax-exempt agricultural bond, a subset of an industrial development bond, for a loan amount that cannot exceed $250,000, according to Wirth. The bond then is privately placed with a local bank, he added.
In fact, Nelson said all loans created by beginning farmer state programs are privately placed and none are sold in the open market.

The exemption from federal income tax payments on interest earned on the loans allows banks to charge lower rates. Wirth said interest rates on the tax-exempt loans average seven percent, compared to nine percent on a conventional loan.
Loan proceeds can be used to purchase land and in some cases equipment, Wirth said.
The amount of loans each state agency can initiate is subject to their federal private activity bond cap allocation. Wirth said his agency is restricted this year to $12 million.

Steve Ferguson, executive director of Iowa Agricultural Development Authority, said the agency had been averaging 20 to 30 loan requests per month. In the wake of the bill signing, the number jumped to 225 requests, he said.
The agency has already completed $19 million of tax-exempt loans this year and can go up to $24 million, which is the agency's limit under its private activity cap allocation.
